content.text: Azure's platform is built with redundancy, but your deployment isn't redundant until you make it so. Availability zones, second regions, higher tiers and backups are features you choose and configure, and a single VM gets a 99.9% SLA, not 99.99%. Even then, the SLA only promises a service credit, and nothing in it protects your data from a bad delete.

A small team moves its booking app from a rented server to Azure: one virtual machine for the API and one for the database, in the same region. The slide for management says "Now on Azure: highly available and backed up". Months later, a power problem in one datacenter takes both VMs offline for most of a morning. While they wait, the manager asks when the last backup ran, and the team discovers that nobody ever turned backups on. Azure behaved exactly as documented. The slide didn't.
The common misconception

The belief: moving an app to a big cloud provider makes it highly available and backed up. Microsoft runs redundant datacenters, so whatever you deploy there inherits that redundancy, and the "99.99%" you've seen on slides applies to your app.

It's convincing because half of it is true. The platform really is redundant: Microsoft's reliability docs describe facilities with "redundant power, cooling, and network connections" and hardware with "redundancy at multiple layers." Some services take more off your plate, too: with SaaS, you "typically don't need to opt into using availability zones".
What's missing is the step between the platform and your app. Redundant hardware under a single VM still leaves you with a single VM.
What actually happens
Responsibility is split in three

Azure's reliability model has three levels. "Microsoft is solely responsible for core platform reliability": facilities, networks, hardware and how updates roll out. The second level is capabilities such as availability zones, multiple regions, service tiers and backups. Microsoft builds them, but "it's your responsibility to evaluate and configure them". The third level is your application, which you design to tolerate faults. The security side of the
shared responsibility model
adds your data: "For all cloud deployment types, you own your data and identities."
So the model doesn't hand reliability to the provider. It hands you the tools.
A resource sits in one zone unless you spread it
Many Azure regions are split into
availability zones

, "separated groups of datacenters within a region", where each one "has independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure." Zones only help the resources that use them: "Some Azure services automatically use multiple zones, while others require you to configure multiple-zone deployment."

That leaves three shapes. A zone-redundant resource is spread across zones by the service, and Microsoft handles the failover. A zonal resource is pinned to one zone you pick, and the docs warn that "zonal deployments don't automatically provide resiliency to availability zone outages." A nonzonal resource, which is what you get when you configure no zones, lands wherever Azure places it, and "if any availability zone in the region experiences an outage, nonzonal resources might be in the affected zone and could experience downtime." The booking app's two VMs were nonzonal.
Zones also have a ceiling: "Availability zones don't protect against a full-region outage." Surviving that takes a second region or a tested backup-and-restore plan, and both are your decisions.
The SLA depends on how you deploy
The
SLA

isn't one number per cloud; it's one number per configuration. The Service Level Agreement for Microsoft Online Services, in its November 1, 2026 edition, sets these uptime levels for virtual machines:

rows.text: Two or more instances across two or more availability zones
Two or more instances in the same availability set
One VM with Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 or Ultra Disk

content.text: Then read what the number buys. Missing it earns a service credit, and "Service Credits are your sole and exclusive remedy for any performance or availability issues". They "will not be awarded to compensate for any other forms of loss, including but not limited to lost revenue".
Dependencies multiply

Your app is up only when everything on its request path is up. The Well-Architected Framework says it in one line: "A composite SLO value is a product distribution of the contributing factors." The booking app needs both VMs, each a single instance on Premium SSD, so its composite is 99.9% × 99.9% = 99.8001%.

For pay-as-you-go VMs, the SLA counts over 30 days: 43,200 minutes. One 99.9% VM may be down 43.2 minutes before a credit is due; the composite allows about 86, before any bug or bad deploy of your own. Spread each tier across two zones and you get 99.99% × 99.99% ≈ 99.98%, about 8.6 minutes. Multiplying assumes the VMs fail independently, so treat the result as an estimate, not a promise.
Replication isn't a backup
Zone redundancy keeps copies in sync, and that includes your mistakes: replication copies every write, so a
DELETE
without a
WHERE

is copied too. That's why the shared responsibility docs list backups separately, as protection "against outages as well as data corruption and other data loss events", and add: "You're responsible for verifying whether backups are enabled and for configuring them appropriately."

rows.text: Azure makes my app highly available
Azure offers zones, regions and tiers; you choose and configure them
Only when instances run in two or more zones
It pays a credit, for one configuration, under conditions
Replication copies mistakes; backups are separate and yours to enable

blocks.title: Zones cost less than you'd think

content.text: The usual objections to spreading across zones are latency and transfer cost. Microsoft aims for inter-zone round-trip latency "of less than approximately 2 milliseconds", and "Azure doesn't charge for data transfer between availability zones in the same region". The real cost is running two or more instances instead of one.

blocks.title: An SLA has conditions, and nobody checks them for you

content.text: The 99.99% applies only while two or more VMs run in two or more zones. One VM alone in an availability set counts as a single-instance VM, and a single VM gets the lowest level of its disks, so one Standard HDD data disk pulls it down to 95%. Checking is on you: "Microsoft doesn't monitor or enforce your eligibility."
How to apply it in your project

For every resource on your request path, write down whether it's zone-redundant, zonal or nonzonal. Each service's reliability guide on Microsoft Learn explains its zone support, and the docs warn: "Don't assume that all tiers or SKUs support availability zones."

items.title: Do the SLA arithmetic for your real setup

content.text: Look up the SLA for each resource's exact configuration (tier, disk type, instance count) and multiply along the request path. If the result is far below what the business expects, that gap is your design discussion.

items.title: Turn on backups and restore one

content.text: Check that every data store has backups enabled, then restore one into a scratch environment. Until a restore has worked, you have backup files, not a recovery plan.

items.title: Decide what happens if the region goes down

content.text: Choose a second region, or a written backup-and-restore plan with recovery targets the business has agreed to. "Accept the risk" is a valid answer; leaving the question blank isn't.
Key takeaways

items.text: Microsoft owns the platform's reliability; you own choosing and configuring zones, regions, tiers and backups.
A resource survives a zone outage only when it runs in two or more zones; a nonzonal VM sits in one place.
SLAs are per configuration: 99.99% for VMs across zones, 99.9% for one VM on Premium SSD (November 2026 edition).
Dependencies multiply: two 99.9% VMs in series give 99.8001%, about 86 minutes of allowed downtime in 30 days.
Replication copies mistakes too; enabling, configuring and test-restoring backups is your job.
